ingredients.intro: A one ingredient list is a short section. Here is the plant, why its Latin name earns its place, the row this label still leaves empty, and the shell.

cards.p: A perennial legume with pinnate leaves and pale pea flowers, from northern China, Mongolia and Korea. Astragalus is one of the largest genera of flowering plants, several thousand species wide, which is why the second half of the name does the work here.

The root is the part normally milled under this name. It is sliced the long way into pale, tongue shaped pieces and tastes faintly sweet. Our listing does not print a part, so this page does not state one.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The species is named in Latin, the count and the milligrams are both printed, the serving is printed, and the day rate is arithmetic you can repeat. The part of the plant is the one row still empty. What astragalus does in a person is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: From Reiss
reiss.h2: Why the Latin matters more on this jar than most
paras: Astragalus is one of the largest genera of flowering plants there is. Several thousand species carry the name, they grow on every continent except Antarctica, and some of them are known to poison grazing stock. The word astragalus on its own tells you almost nothing. Astragalus membranaceus tells you which plant.

That is the whole argument for printing a binomial, and it is why the row above gives the name the listing prints and then adds that some catalogues file it under mongholicus. Two names, one plant, and you should be able to see both from the sheet rather than find out later.

The listing this jar came from carries a stack of study links. There are no study links on this page. What I can give you is the species, 800 mg a capsule, 50 capsules, two a day with lunch, and the fact that nobody here has yet written down which part of the plant was milled.
reiss.pull: The word astragalus on its own tells you almost nothing.
